title: Predicting IGD treatment outcomes across interventions using a whole-brain functional connectome biomarker.
authors: Wei M, Luo X, Fu J, Li S, Ni H, Liu J, Dong GH
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although treatment approaches have been explored in internet gaming disorder (IGD), however, little is known about the specific neural activity that is associated with treatment outcomes. This study aims to establish a treatment-sensitive network that reliably predicts treatment outcomes across different interventions for IGD. METHODS: Resting-state fMRI data were collected from 90 individuals with IGD who received one of three different intervention protocols (mindfulness meditation, approach bias modification, or retrieval-aversive conditioning training). Connectome-based predictive modelling (CPM) was used to build a treatment-sensitive network to predict individual symptom reduction, then validated them on the external dataset. RESULTS: The negative (r = 0.401, p <.001) and combined network (r = 0.480, p <.001) can significantly predict a reduction of addiction severity (baseline minus post-test). Specifically, the negative network was primarily centred on the motor, subcortical, and salience networks. The positive network primarily involved cerebellar-related connections. Incorporating these into a combined model significantly improved predictive accuracy, suggesting that cerebellar-related connectivity may contribute to the prediction of intervention-related clinical improvement. Finally, the treatment-sensitive network was validated in a separate data. CONCLUSIONS: This study established a treatment-sensitive network based on the whole-brain connectome. These findings provide valuable empirical evidence for identifying biomarkers for IGD treatment and advance personalised therapeutic strategies. CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTRATION: The trial protocol was pre-registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (www.chictr.org.cn; ChiCTR2300077831(MM), ChiCTR2300075869(ApBm), ChiCTR2500095444(R-AC), ChiCTR2400090834(SAE)).

title: Evaluating a Modified American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status-Based Sedation Management System for Pancreatobiliary Endoscopy: A Prospective Feasibility Study.
authors: Hanaoka T, Okuwaki K, Watanabe M, Matsuda H, Adachi K, Tamaki A, Ogawa D, Sakai M
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To prospectively evaluate the feasibility of implementing a modified American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status (ASA-PS)-based sedation management system for endoscopist-managed sedation in pancreatobiliary endoscopy. METHODS: This single-center, single-arm prospective feasibility study involved 2000 patients (2024-2025). Sedation risk was stratified using a modified ASA-PS classification system combined with predefined high-risk clinical factors (severe obesity, obstructive sleep apnea requiring continuous positive airway pressure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease requiring home oxygen therapy, reduced functional capacity, and difficult sedation history). Patients meeting high-risk criteria underwent pre-procedural anesthesiologist assessment to determine sedation providers. The primary outcome was sedation-related adverse event (SRAE) incidence during endoscopist-managed sedation. The secondary outcomes were the sedation success rate and SRAE-associated risk factors. RESULTS: Among 2000 patients, 231 (11.6%) were classified as having high risk for sedation. Post-assessment, anesthesiologists and endoscopists managed sedation for 86 (4.3%) and 1914 (95.7%) patients, respectively. In the endoscopist-managed group, SRAEs occurred in 63 patients (3.3%), corresponding to a success rate of 96.7%. No patient required tracheal intubation or conversion to general anesthesia. In multivariable analysis, endoscopic ultrasonography-guided sampling was independently associated with reduced SRAEs (odds ratio 0.407, 95% confidence interval 0.184-0.899; p = 0.026); no independent predictors of increased SRAEs were identified. CONCLUSIONS: The modified ASA-PS-based sedation management system may be a feasible approach in settings with limited anesthesiology resources, warranting further validation. title: Associations of 24-hour movement behavior composition with depressive symptoms and problematic internet use in Chinese adolescents: A cohort study.
authors: Fang B, Sun Y, Bai Y, Liu WJ, Lin R, Xia W
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Although 24-hour movement behaviors (24-HMB), including sleep, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), and screen time, are associated with adolescent mental health, their compositional nature remains insufficiently examined. We investigated the associations of 24-HMB composition with depressive symptoms, problematic internet use (PIU), and their co-occurrence at one-year follow-up. METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, 12,316 adolescents from the Guangzhou Childhood Adolescent Cohort (2019-2025) were included. Baseline sleep duration, screen time, depressive symptoms, and PIU were assessed using questionnaires, and MVPA was estimated from the number of days per week with at least 60 min of activity. After 1 year of follow-up, outcome-specific analytic samples included 9887 adolescents for depressive symptoms, 11,622 for PIU, and 12,316 for co-occurrence, with 2169, 1149, and 845 events, respectively. Nonlinear associations were examined using restricted cubic splines, and stratified compositional logistic regression models and exploratory isotemporal substitution analyses were then conducted using outcome-specific sleep-duration thresholds identified from the fitted spline curves. RESULTS: Sleep showed nonlinear associations, with the predicted odds reaching its nadir at 8.50 h/day for depressive symptoms, 8.81 h/day for PIU, and 8.68 h/day for co-occurrence. The associations of 24-HMB composition differed across sleep-duration strata for depressive symptoms (P for interaction = 0.014), PIU (P for interaction < 0.001), and co-occurrence (P for interaction = 0.004). Among adolescents sleeping below the outcome-specific thresholds, relatively longer sleep was associated with lower odds of depressive symptoms (OR = 0.53, 95% CI: 0.37-0.76), PIU (OR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.22-0.50), and co-occurrence (OR = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.32-0.79), particularly when replacing screen time. In the lower-sleep strata, relatively longer screen time was associated with higher odds of these outcomes, whereas theoretical reallocations from screen time to the estimated MVPA component were associated with lower odds in exploratory substitution analyses. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings highlight the importance of considering 24-HMB as an integrated composition. The associations of 24-HMB reallocations with mental health outcomes differed across sleep-duration strata. Reducing screen time, with reallocation to sleep or MVPA according to sleep-duration strata, may offer tailored strategies to improve adolescent mental health.

title: The application progress of detection technology for Bacillus cereus in food: Challenges, innovations and future prospects.
authors: Zhang Y, Zhang X, Zheng H, Wang H, Yu M, Jia W, Jia Z, Cui J
abstract: Food safety is a key issue of global public health. As a foodborne pathogen - Bacillus cereus (B. cereus), it is widely distributed in nature and can cause diseases in both humans and animals. The rapid detection of B. cereus is of great significance for the prevention and control of such diseases. This article provides a detailed overview of the development of B. cereus detection techniques in food, transitioning from traditional methods to a series of current technologies such as immunology, molecular biology and MALDI-TOF-MS. The principles, advantages and disadvantages of various detection techniques, as well as their application progress, were outlined. Furthermore, the application and advantages of combining different techniques in the detection of B. cereus in food were demonstrated. The CRISPR/Cas system possesses the characteristics of high specificity, high sensitivity and ease of operation, and shows great potential in the field of foodborne pathogen detection. This article also explains that the combination of CRISPR/Cas technology with RPA, LFA and AI technologies can further enhance the detection rate and accuracy. The aforementioned technology can enable the early detection and prevention of B. cereus in food, ensuring food safety and preventing the outbreak of foodborne diseases. This article has certain reference value in the research on the detection techniques of B. cereus and other foodborne pathogens in food, and provides strong support for safeguarding food safety and maintaining human health.

title: Advances and perspectives in genetically encoded biosensors for biomarker detection and theranostic circuits.
authors: Xu J, Qi Q, Wang Q
abstract: Effective biomarker detection is critical for timely and accurate clinical disease diagnosis. However, conventional analytical methodologies are often constrained by laborious procedures, reliance on specialized equipment, and an inherent inability to perform continuous in situ monitoring. To circumvent these limitations, synthetic biology has pioneered the development of genetically encoded biosensors as a rapid, highly sensitive, and cost-effective alternative. This review specifically focuses on transcriptional regulation-based biosensors, primarily those utilizing allosteric transcription factors (aTFs) and two-component systems (TCSs). By integrating these regulatory sensing modules into engineered microbial chassis, researchers can achieve continuous, real-time biomarker monitoring even within complex and otherwise inaccessible physiological environments. This review particularly focuses on microbial chassis rather than mammalian systems due to their highly tractable genetics, rapid response kinetics, and their unique potential to be deployed as autonomous living probiotics for in situ theranostics. Furthermore, coupling these sensors with engineered actuator genes enables the construction of intelligent therapeutic genetic circuits. This closed-loop theranostic paradigm facilitates simultaneous, real-time diagnosis and autonomous, localized therapeutic interventions, paving the way for personalized and dose-adaptive precision medicine. Finally, we summarize recent advancements in these biosensor platforms, explore their applications in targeted disease interventions, and discuss the contemporary challenges alongside future perspectives for their clinical translation.

title: Therapeutic Balloon-Assisted Enteroscopy: Recent Advances in the Management of Small Bowel Diseases.
authors: Nagayama M, Kinoshita T, Kawaguchi H, Fujinuma T, Fujikura S, Hayashi H, Tamaru T, Sakamoto H
abstract: Balloon-assisted enteroscopy (BAE) has substantially advanced small bowel disease management. This review summarizes recent therapeutic BAE advances, focusing on three major indications: small bowel vascular lesions, hereditary polyposis syndromes, and Crohn's disease (CD). For suspected small bowel bleeding from vascular lesions, morphological classification guides lesion-specific hemostasis-primarily using argon plasma coagulation and clipping-while gel immersion endoscopy helps secure the visual field. In hereditary polyposis syndromes (e.g., Peutz-Jeghers syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis), endoscopic ischemic and cold snare polypectomy prevent intussusception and reduce cancer risk, decreasing surgical needs. Additionally, endoscopic balloon dilation is an established bowel-preserving treatment for fibrotic CD strictures, reducing surgical resection and short bowel syndrome risk. Driven by evolving imaging and devices, BAE remains central to small bowel management, improving patient outcomes and quality of life.

title: Ultrasound-responsive nanotherapy promotes axonal regeneration after SCI via reactivating CREB/miR-129-5p signaling.
authors: Gu G, Zhu H, Li S, Zhang Z, Kao Y, Zhang R, Fu R, Han X
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) remains a devastating neurological disorder with few effective therapeutic interventions due to the poor intrinsic regenerative capacity of adult central nervous system neurons. Here, we identified miR-129-5p as a downstream effector of cAMP-response element binding protein (CREB) signaling that promotes axonal growth by suppressing glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK3β). Leveraging this regenerative mechanism, we developed a low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU)-responsive biomimetic nanoplatform (CM-miR-CNP@PFP) for targeted SCI therapy. The platform comprises miR-129-5p/perfluoropentane (PFP)-loaded cationic lipid nanoparticles (CNPs) coated with hybrid membranes from RVG-engineered human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells and macrophages. The biomimetic coating grants superior immune evasion, prolonged circulation, and precise neuronal targeting. Under local LIFU irradiation, CM-miR-CNP@PFP undergoes acoustic droplet vaporization (ADV), a liquid-to-gas phase transition that enhances lesion-site accumulation and cellular delivery of miR-129-5p. In vivo, this ultrasound-responsive therapy significantly attenuated astroglial and fibrotic scar-associated changes, promoted axonal regeneration, and improved motor function. Overall, this biomimetic nanoplatform represents a promising strategy for targeted miRNA delivery and neural regeneration after SCI, with potential for further translational development.

title: Neuroimaging Biomarkers for Brain Disorder Diagnosis Using Advanced Learning Techniques.
authors: Ion IA, Chira C
abstract: Mental illness is becoming increasingly common in everyday life, affecting a growing number of people. Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) is an effective technique for detecting mental disorders. Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) analyses spontaneous low-frequency oscillations in the Blood Oxygen Level Dependent signal to examine the functional architecture of the brain. fMRI and rs-fMRI data processing contribute to mapping neural activity in specific brain regions, enabling accurate localization of cognitive functions and improving our understanding of Functional Connectivity and interactions among brain regions. This paper focuses on the use of Machine Learning and Deep Learning techniques for fMRI analysis to identify brain features that may be associated with Bipolar Disorder (BD) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD). The first step in the proposed approach is the preprocessing of fMRI and rs-fMRI data using two distinct methods: the first combines Statistical Parametric Mapping and the CONN toolbox for improved results, and the second focuses on the MELODIC software. The proposed approach begins with fMRI and rs-fMRI preprocessing using two pipelines: one integrating Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM) with the CONN toolbox and another based on the MELODIC framework. The aim is to evaluate how preprocessing choices affect functional connectivity representations and classification performance when combined with classical Machine Learning (ML) methods, namely Support Vector Machines and Random Forests, and the Deep Learning (DL) model AlexNet. Given the altered brain connectivity patterns observed in Bipolar Disorder and Alzheimer's Disease, these methods are employed to assess preprocessing-learning interactions across both disorders. Experimental results emphasize that Connbox-SPM preprocessing combined with AlexNet yields the best results for both mental disorders, with Bipolar Disorder reporting 78.2% accuracy and AD achieving 82.4% accuracy.

title: Discovering Heterogeneous Neurodegenerative Disease Patterns From MRI Data for Improved Prediction.
authors: Zhang Y, Li H, Fan Y
journal: Medical image computing and computer-assisted intervention : MICCAI ... International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases exhibit substantial heterogeneity, complicating both diagnosis and prognosis. Identifying clinically meaningful subtypes is crucial for understanding disease mechanisms and improving diagnostic precision and prognostic accuracy. Existing subtyping approaches primarily rely on unsupervised learning of patient data for capturing inter-individual variability, but they may fail to uncover subtypes that are directly informative for diagnosis or prognosis. To address this limitation, we propose a novel mixture-of-experts (MoE) framework that integrates predictive modeling with subtype discovery. Unlike traditional subtyping methods, our approach learns a router to assign individuals to specialized expert networks, each corresponding to a distinct subtype, for improving predictive accuracy. By coupling subtype identification with prediction, the proposed MoE framework encourages the discovery of subtypes that are not only statistically distinct but also clinically informative. We evaluate the framework on a real-world dataset of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) subjects and a semi-simulated dataset, demonstrating superior performance in predicting progression from MCI to Alzheimer's disease while revealing distinct, clinically meaningful MCI subtypes. Code is available at https://github.com/Kateridge/MoESubtyping.

title: Long-term monitoring reveals immobility-defined sleep fragmentation and behavioural alterations in collagen-induced arthritis mouse model of both sexes.
authors: Macáková K, Szabó J, Skybová E, Vlková B, Borbélyová V, Celec P
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease that impairs musculoskeletal function and overall well-being, often disrupting sleep and worsening cognitive and behavioural outcomes. While animal models of collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) are widely used, sleep behaviour in arthritic mice remains poorly studied. This study aimed to evaluate immobility-defined sleep behaviour in the CIA mouse model using continuous, non-invasive, long-term monitoring (LTM). CIA was induced in 12-month-old DBA/1 J mice (females: n = 13; males: n = 17) using type II collagen and complete Freund's adjuvant. On day 63 post-induction, immobility-defined sleep behaviour was recorded over 12 h (6-hour rest and 6-hour active phase) in PhenoTyper cages. Behavioural tests included open field, novel object recognition, reciprocal interaction, and nesting. During the rest phase of LTM, CIA mice showed 50% less immobility-defined sleep time, shorter sleep bouts, and more frequent sleep interruptions, while in the active phase of LTM, CIA mice showed 50% reduced locomotor activity as well. They also showed worse short-term memory, 50% higher anxiety-like behaviour, 5-fold more self-grooming, and up to 80% less exploration than controls. CIA mice showed 50% less social interactions than controls, while CIA females spent more time in feeding and drinking zones. In CIA mice, more frequent interruptions of immobility-defined sleep were associated with higher arthritis scores, while associations with reduced nest building and rearing, elevated self-grooming, and larger hind-paw volume were moderate, but did not survive multiple testing corrections. Overall, CIA mice showed altered immobility-defined sleep continuity alongside broader functional deficits, some of which were sex-specific. These findings support LTM as a complementary approach to characterising sleep-related and behavioural alterations in experimental arthritis, and open new avenues for exploring the role of sleep in the overall well-being of patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

title: Gut microbiota and metabolic characteristics in PWHIV with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).
authors: Liu H, Xu T, Guo Y, Zhou X, Yan C, Zhu B, Xie Y
abstract: The global prevalence of Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) among persons with HIV (PWHIV) is estimated at 34%. This study examined the influence of gut microbial and metabolic alterations in PWHIV with MASLD. We conducted 16S rRNA sequencing on 60 fecal samples (24 from HIV group and 36 from HIV-MASLD group) to assess microbial composition, and employed LC/MS-based metabolomics on both fecal and plasma samples to identify variations in metabolites. An exploratory analysis was performed to compare plasma cytokines and oxidative stress markers between the two groups. Sequencing in the HIV-MASLD group showed lower Faecalibacterium and Anaerobutyricum, and higher Klebsiella, Escherichia, and Enterococcus. Metabolomic analysis revealed a reduction in anti-inflammatory metabolites (Dodecanedioic acid, 5-Phenylvaleric acid, Kynurenic acid) and antioxidant metabolites, coupled with an increase in the pro-inflammatory metabolite Gamma-Glutamyl-L-Putrescine in the HIV-MASLD group. And plasma analysis indicated a decline in 20-carboxy arachidonic acid. Additionally, Faecalibacterium and Anaerobutyricum correlated positively with anti-inflammatory metabolites, while Klebsiella, Enterobacter, and Citrobacter correlated negatively. Furthermore, Faecalibacterium and Anaerobutyricum also showed a moderate negative correlation with MDA levels. A random forest model using plasma metabolites showed the optimal discriminative ability for HIV-MASLD (AUC = 0.819 ± 0.0059). Differences in gut microbiota and metabolites in PWHIV may affect MASLD progression by influencing inflammation and oxidative stress. Modulating gut microbiota, such as adding Faecalibacterium and Anaerobutyricum, could be a treatment strategy for HIV-MASLD. Plasma metabolites have potential as noninvasive markers.

title: Systems metabolic engineering of a plasmid-free Escherichia coli cell factory for high-level cytidine production.
authors: Zhao R, Li C, Xu C, Chen Z, Xiong H, Yu Z, Shi T, Li L
abstract: Cytidine is an important precursor for nucleoside pharmaceuticals, but its fermentative production is constrained by competing degradation, poor selectivity of pyrimidine flux, insufficient precursor supply, and energy-redox imbalance. In this study, a plasmid-free E. coli cell factory was constructed through systems metabolic engineering. Sequential deletion of cytidine degradation, salvage, and precursor-consuming pathways enabled initial cytidine accumulation. The conversion from UMP to CMP was strengthened by introducing feedback-deregulated pyrH D93A and pyrG D160E, E162A, E168K cgl mutants and nudG, while the heterologous expression of PHM8 sce improved CMP-to-cytidine conversion selectivity. Scaffold-based assembly of PyrF, PyrHD93A, NudG, and PHM8sce using CipA/CipB further improved local pathway channeling and reduced uridine formation by 98.70%. To reinforce upstream flux, de novo UMP biosynthesis was reconstructed with the B. subtilis pyr operon, PRPP synthesis was enhanced, and nitrogen-donor and pyrimidine-ring precursor supply was improved through glnA, ppc, and aspC expression. Finally, an ATP-responsive ydaO motif regulatory module was used to dynamically control respiratory-chain and oxygen-utilization modules, coordinating ATP supply with NAD+ regeneration. The final strain cyt 23 produced 96.20 g/L cytidine in 50 h in a 5 L fed-batch bioreactor, with a glucose conversion yield of 0.38 g/g and productivity of 1.92 g/(L·h), representing the highest reported titer, yield and productivity for microbial cytidine production to date. This work provides an integrated strategy for high-level microbial cytidine production and nucleoside cell-factory development.

title: Microbial succession and genome-resolved metabolic functions shape flavor evolution during sauce-flavor Baijiu fermentation.
authors: Niu J, Li W, Chen X, Zhu H, Sun W, Li X, Sun B
abstract: Sauce-flavor Baijiu (SFB) fermentation is characterized by a unique multi-round solid-state process, during which complex microbial succession drives flavor formation. However, the functional differentiation and metabolic mechanisms of microbial communities across successive fermentation rounds remain poorly understood. In this study, the physicochemical properties, microbial assembly, and metabolic profiles of fermented grains (FG) were investigated across seven production rounds (R1-R7). The results revealed that as fermentation rounds progressed, the FG environment evolved toward elevated acidity and reduced pH, driving a directional shift in the microbial community from an initially diverse assemblage to a structure dominated by acid-tolerant Acetilactobacillus, which established pronounced ecological dominance in later rounds. Metabolomic analysis further indicated that this dynamic adjustment of microbial structure drove the evolution of the flavor profile, specifically manifesting as differential accumulation of compounds such as esters, alcohols, and pyrazines across the various rounds. Co-occurrence network analysis demonstrated that positive microbial interactions significantly predominated within the fermentation system, and that community function exhibited a convergent trend as the rounds increased. Furthermore, 158 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) were recovered, and metabolic reconstruction elucidated the potential contributions of genera such as Pediococcus, Bacillus, and Oceanobacillus to key metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, phenylalanine metabolism, and pyrazine biosynthesis. This work provides important insights into microbial regulation and quality improvement in SFB fermentation.

title: Multi-omics and functional validation profiling reveals the regulatory mechanism of biofilm-forming Tetragenococcus halophilus JY1 in response to salt tolerance.
authors: Zhao C, Sun D, Li S, Lu X, Liu X, Mu Y, Luo L
abstract: Biofilms are crucial for enhancing microbial productivity in industrial applications, yet the mechanisms underlying their stress resistance and formation in functional microorganisms remain inadequately explored. Tetragenococcus halophilus, a halophilic lactic acid bacterium, is widely utilized in traditional fermentation industries; however, research has focused on its planktonic state. To address this gap, this study investigated the molecular mechanisms of biofilm formation in T. halophilus JY1 under low-salt (0.2 M, LS) and high-salt (3 M, HS) stress conditions. Physiological analyses revealed that biofilms protected cellular integrity under LS and HS, as evidenced by marked elevations in ATPase activity and ATP concentration. Furthermore, salt stress altered the abundance and composition of JY1 biofilms. RNA-seq analysis identified upregulation of genes associated with cell surface composition, energy homeostasis, and ion transport. Metabolomic profiling further revealed elevated levels of glycerophospholipids and fatty acids in JY1 under LS and HS. Functional validation further demonstrated that overexpression of ohrR, yodB, isaA, icaA, ruvA, and ctsR significantly promoted biofilm formation in recombinant strains. In addition, exogenous monounsaturated fatty acids (C16:1, C14:1, and C20:1) markedly improved cell survival and biofilm formation under salt stress by modulating membrane lipid composition and enhancing osmotic adaptation. Overall, restructuring of biofilms emerged as a key adaptive strategy for JY1 in response to salinity, while prolonged salt exposure reduced physiological and metabolic activity. This study provides critical insights into the adaptive strategies of biofilm-forming microorganisms and opens new avenues for the application of biofilms in industrial processes.

title: Salt-dependent osmoadaptation and metabolic responses of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum BS3-1 in fermented bamboo shoots.
authors: Xie L, Zhang X, Shen K, Wang X, Zhou S
abstract: Salt concentration shapes the growth and metabolism of lactic acid bacteria in vegetable fermentations, yet the effects of salt gradients on the fermentation performance of suansun-derived Lactiplantibacillus plantarum BS3-1, together with associated temporal transcriptional changes in BS3-1 and metabolite variation in the fermentation broth, remain insufficiently characterized. Here, BS3-1 was evaluated across a 0-7% (w/w) salt gradient during suansun fermentation. The 0%, 3%, and 5% treatments were selected for time-series transcriptomic analysis of fermentation-derived cell pellets and untargeted metabolomic analysis of fermentation-broth supernatants. The 3% treatment yielded the highest sensory score (79.0/100 versus 72.2/100 in the no-added-salt treatment). On day 7, total acidity was 8.16 g/L at 1% salt and 3.60 g/L at 7%, and viable cells at 7% fell below the detection limit. BS3-1 transcriptional profiles and fermentation-broth metabolite compositions differed among salt treatments. In the 3% versus 0% comparison, 119 differentially expressed genes were shared across four time points, while an average of 598 differential metabolites was identified per time point. WGCNA identified 17 co-expression modules with significant module-trait associations. Association analysis integrating 126 candidate hub genes from four phenotype-associated modules with 30 shared differential metabolites retained 1100 gene-metabolite associations (|r| ≥ 0.65, global BH-FDR < 0.05). Overall, under the tested conditions, 3% salt provided the most favorable balance among viable-cell persistence, acidification, and sensory quality, while multi-omics analysis revealed covariation among BS3-1 transcriptional responses, fermentation traits, and fermentation-broth metabolite variation.

title: Alzheimer's disease-associated presenilin 2 N141I mutation impairs neuronal lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial dynamics through selective downregulation of the Golgi exchange factor Gbf1.
authors: Saleki S, Wabant C, Loriot A, Stanga S, Masquelier J, Muccioli GG, Suelves N, Kienlen-Campard P
abstract: Presenilin 2 (PS2) mutations cause familial Alzheimer's disease, yet their effects beyond amyloid processing remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how PS2 deletion and the N141I mutation affect neuronal lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial dynamics in mouse primary neurons. Both PS2 deletion and N141I mutation reduced neuronal lipid content. However, exogenous lipid supplementation rescued this deficit only in N141I-expressing neurons, indicating a partial loss-of-function effect. N141I neurons also displayed reduced OPA1, a mitochondrial fusion regulator, restored by lipid supplementation. RNA-sequencing identified Gbf1, a Golgi-specific guanine nucleotide exchange factor, as selectively downregulated in N141I but not knockout tissue, which was confirmed at the protein level in mouse brain and primary neurons. Gbf1 knockdown in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) recapitulated the N141I lipid profile. Together, these findings reveal a PS2-GBF1-lipid-mitochondria axis disrupted specifically by the N141I mutation, suggesting an amyloid-independent pathway contributing to neurodegeneration and identifying potential therapeutic targets for familial Alzheimer's disease.

title: Synthesis and pharmacological evaluation of a series of fluoro-substituted 3-phenoxy-azetidines as cortical enhancers for the treatment of apathy.
authors: Sonesson C, von Unge S, Gullme M, Rousk L, Fagerberg A, Knubbe T, Svanberg B, Ljung E
abstract: We here report the discovery of a series of fluoro-substituted 3-phenoxy-azetidines useful for modulating levels of monoamines in cerebral cortical areas of the brain. The compounds were characterized by in vivo studies using, in particular, behavioural, and microdialysis methods. Furthermore, the compounds were tested in binding assays for the human serotonin (5-HT), noradrenaline (NA), and dopamine (DA) transporters in order to assess the risk for addiction/dependency. Optimization of this class of compounds for improving cognitive functions while minimizing the effect on monoamine transporters resulted in the selection of a candidate drug 1 (IRL757). After 1 was successfully assessed in different animal models for motivation/goal-directed behaviour (unpublished data), it is currently being evaluated in humans for the treatment of apathy in neurological disorders in general, and in particular in Parkinson's disease (PD).

title: Synchronous and Metachronous Multiple Gastric Epithelial Neoplasms Detected During Index Evaluation and Post-Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection Surveillance: A Descriptive Comparison.
authors: Yoshio T, Fukunaga S, Nakane T, Minami S, Cho T, Tsuruta K, Tanaka H, Gotou R
abstract: OBJECTIVES: We compared synchronous and metachronous gastric tumors detected during index evaluation and surveillance after endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), focusing on Kimura-Takemoto O-3 atrophy. Helicobacter pylori eradication history and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) were exploratory. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients who underwent ESD. Patients whose first additional lesion was detected simultaneously or within 1 year after index ESD were classified as having synchronous gastric tumors (SGT); those with no synchronous lesion whose first additional lesion was detected later were classified as having metachronous gastric tumors (MGT). Logistic regression estimated associations with SGT rather than MGT presentation. RESULTS: Among 1064 screened patients, 256 had multiple lesions (SGT, n = 169; MGT, n = 87). SGT patients were older (median, 76 vs. 72 years; p = 0.005), and O-3 atrophy was more frequent (34.3% vs. 20.5%; p = 0.045). In exploratory multivariable analysis, age (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.67 per 10 years; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.12-2.51) and O-3 atrophy (aOR, 2.17; 95% CI, 1.01-4.65) were associated with SGT presentation. Eradication timing was unavailable, and NLR was not independently associated with SGT. CONCLUSIONS: O-3 atrophy was more frequent when the first additional lesion was detected synchronously. SGT and MGT may represent timing-defined phenotypes within a continuous atrophic field rather than biologically distinct entities. Extensive atrophy supports meticulous whole-stomach inspection at index evaluation and sustained surveillance.

title: Clinical Outcomes of Rubber-clip-assisted Versus Conventional Colorectal Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection: A Retrospective Study.
authors: Uyama K, Iwagami H, Akamatsu T, Sakano R, Kitada T, Shimoyama M, Terashita T, Nakatani Y
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Adequate traction is essential for safe and efficient colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), but gravitational traction is often insufficient in certain situations. Several traction techniques are reportedly effective. We use the rubber-clip method (RCM), which is a simple and inexpensive technique that combines a standard clip with a rubber band to allow directional traction adjustment. This study was performed to evaluate the clinical outcomes of RCM-assisted colorectal ESD. METHODS: Among 551 colorectal ESD procedures performed between January 2014 and October 2025, 452 patients were eligible for inclusion. Propensity score matching using seven covariates yielded 56 RCM and 56 non-RCM cases. The primary endpoint was procedure time, and the secondary endpoints were perforation, bleeding, en bloc resection, and pathological complete resection. Additionally, all procedures were classified as long-duration (≥120 min) or short-duration (<120 min) to identify independent risk factors for prolonged procedures, including intraoperative variables. RESULTS: After matching, the RCM group showed a significantly shorter procedure time than the non-RCM group (66.8 vs. 90.7 min, respectively; p = 0.024) and a lower perforation rate (0.0 % vs. 10.7%, respectively; p = 0.027). In the multivariate analysis, absence of traction, non-expert endoscopist, moderate-to-severe fibrosis, large lesion size, and poor maneuverability were independent risk factors for prolonged procedures, with absence of traction showing the strongest association. CONCLUSIONS: The RCM shortened procedure time and reduced perforation risk. Given its low cost, simplicity, and ability to adjust traction direction, the RCM may represent an effective traction method for colorectal ESD. UNLABELLED: Trial Registration: N/A.

title: Submucosal Invasion and Ulceration in Early Gastric Cancer Affect Mucosal Impedance.
authors: Miyashiro K, Sawada Y, Kikuchi H, Goto S, Yoshizawa T, Nakano S, Asari T, Tetsuya T
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate early changes in gastric cancers that are difficult to evaluate using endoscopic imaging through the assessment of mucosal impedance (MI) in endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) specimens. METHODS: In this single-center prospective cohort study, we included patients who underwent ESD for early gastric cancer (EGC). MI was measured at both the main tumor site and the surrounding non-neoplastic mucosa in resected specimens. Histopathological evaluation and immunohistochemical staining for claudin-3, -4, and -18 were performed. Furthermore, multivariate analysis was used to investigate factors influencing MI-L. RESULTS: The MI measured under high-frequency current (MI-H) of the non-neoplastic mucosa was significantly higher than that of the tumor (p = 0.0025). Additionally, the MI measured under low-frequency current (MI-L) was significantly lower in pT1b cases than in pT1a cases (6.9 Ω vs. 9.7 Ω, p = 0.021). Similarly, the MI-L was significantly lower in the pUL1 cases than in the pUL0 cases (7.5 Ω vs. 9.7 Ω, p = 0.030). Multivariable linear regression analysis demonstrated that, among the explanatory variables-including tumor invasion, ulcer status, macroscopic type, and the H-scores for each claudin- only the H-score of claudin-18 was identified as an independent associated factor. CONCLUSIONS: In resected specimens, MI-L was independently associated with claudin-18 expression and correlated with submucosal invasion, ulcer status, and macroscopic type. MI has the potential to detect non-surface changes involving tight junction proteins in EGC that cannot be observed via endoscopy. UNLABELLED: Trial Registration: N/A.

title: The ups and downs of human UNC93B1: Autoimmune and viral conditions.
authors: Idiiatullina E, Casanova JL, Zhang SY
abstract: Mouse Unc93b1 was identified in 2006 by forward genetics as an ER membrane protein essential for the activity of the endosomal nucleic acid-sensing receptors TLR3, TLR7, and TLR9. In vitro studies in mouse and human cells have revealed its cellular functions, including ER-based stabilization and trafficking of endosomal TLR proteins (TLR3, TLR7, TLR8, and TLR9) and regulation of signaling thresholds through competitive trafficking control (TLR7 and TLR9). Human genetic studies have clarified the physiological role of UNC93B1 in natural conditions. Biallelic loss-of-function UNC93B1 mutations impair TLR3 signaling in central nervous system-resident cells, thereby conferring a predisposition to HSV-1 encephalitis. UNC93B1 deficiency may also predispose to other viral infections, as suggested by patients with inherited TLR3 or TLR7 deficiency. Conversely, monoallelic or biallelic UNC93B1 gain-of-function variants enhancing TLR7 and/or TLR8 signaling predispose patients to autoimmunity and inflammation, including early-onset systemic lupus erythematosus and chilblain lupus. Thus, in humans, UNC93B1 maintains a delicate balance between host defense and tolerance to self.

title: Genotype-phenotype analysis in 333 individuals with heterozygous variants in NFKB1.
authors: Armbruster SM, Caballero-Oteyza A, Bartsch O, Lorenzini T, Abolhassani H, Chan S, González Granado LI, Garcia-Bustos V
abstract: Heterozygous germline variants in NFKB1 can be classified into variants with "known protein defect" and "unknown protein effect." However, beyond this, NFKB1 variants may be additionally categorized into at least eight distinct variant classes. We conducted a literature review of 67 papers reporting on NFKB1 variants and included four additional individuals, carrying previously unreported NFKB1 variants. We identified 333 individuals with unique variants in NFKB1. Our compiled data revealed that there is no sex predilection, the penetrance-including all heterozygous carriers-was 78%, and the mean age of onset for the "known protein defect cohort" was 21.2 years. Individuals harboring variants with a known protein defect demonstrated a higher frequency of malignancies and autoimmune disorders. However, these individuals were less frequently classified as affected than individuals with variants with unknown protein defect. Carriers of whole NFKB1 gene deletions had a significantly higher penetrance to being designated as "affected," but beyond this, the clinical manifestations did not differ between variant classes.

title: Disease associations for rare immune genetic variants require statistical or rule-based support.
authors: Gray PE, Tangye SG, Kirk EP
abstract: Validating weak gene-disease associations requires statistical support from large case-control studies. In contrast, strong (e.g., monogenic) gene-disease associations may be established from relatively few affected individuals, when independent orthogonal evidence converges. Here, we examine four publications associating heterozygous variants in five genes-TNIP1, P2RY8, BLK, BANK1, and SH2B3-with autoimmune disease (predominantly systemic lupus erythematosus [SLE]). While we do not dispute the molecular findings of these studies, we do not accept the proposed disease associations, which lack case-control evidence and where high minor allele frequencies in non-disease populations, indicate that the genotypes are far too common to represent Mendelian disease alleles. Additionally, 8 of 18 alleles were searchable in UK Biobank, and none showed enrichment in SLE. Until further evidence emerges, caution is warranted in ascribing disease association to heterozygous genotypes in TNIP1, P2RY8, BLK, BANK1, and SH2B3, and linkage to patients in clinical pedigrees should not be taken as inferring a monoallelic inborn error of immunity.

title: Integrated SEM, TEM and CLSM workflow for tegumental analysis of adult Schistosoma mansoni.
authors: de Carvalho Augusto R, João RCF, Barbosa HS, Mello-Silva CC, Santos CP
abstract: The tegument of Schistosoma mansoni is a key host-parasite interface and a major target for drug and vaccine development. Although ultrastructural studies of the tegument date back decades, methodological inconsistencies often complicate comparisons across studies. Here, we present a standardized, easy-to-use framework for investigating tegumental architecture using three complementary techniques: scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM). We provide step-by-step protocols, highlight strengths and limitations of each method, and illustrate their outputs using adult male worms. We also outline a scheme for unbiased quantitative analysis of the resulting images and indicate how the protocols can be adapted to female worms, to other developmental stages and schistosome species, and to immunolocalization at the ultrastructural level. This integrative pipeline enables reproducible morphological characterization and facilitates downstream applications in pharmacology, immunology, and parasite biology.

Integrated proteomic characterization of maternal blood, umbilical cord blood and placental tissue in gestational diabetes mellitus.
authors: Jia X, Wu Q, Li Y, Zhang X, Ye H, Hu X, Chen Y, Wu H
abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes, but molecular alterations across the maternal-placental-fetal interface remain incompletely defined. We applied data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry to matched maternal blood (MB), umbilical cord blood (UCB) and placental tissue collected at delivery from 28 women with GDM and 21 controls. Differential protein abundance analysis, Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment analysis, gene set enrichment analysis, weighted co-expression network analysis and pathway-level corroboration using two independent public placental transcriptomic cohorts were performed. Proteomic changes were compartment specific. Placental tissue showed the greatest number of differentially abundant proteins, whereas maternal blood and umbilical cord blood showed more limited alterations. Exploratory pathway-level analyses in MB suggested metabolic stress- and extracellular matrix-related patterns, whereas UCB suggested immune- and coagulation-related patterns. Placental tissue showed more prominent alterations involving extracellular matrix remodeling and ribosome-related pathways. A GDM-associated placental co-expression module contained both extracellular matrix proteins and ribosomal proteins. Independent transcriptomic datasets provided additional pathway-level support for ribosome-related and inflammatory processes. These findings suggest that GDM is associated with distinct proteomic changes in maternal blood, umbilical cord blood and placental tissue at delivery, with the most prominent alterations involving placental extracellular matrix remodeling and ribosome-related processes. SIGNIFICANCE: This matched multi-compartment proteomic study provides a placenta-centered view of GDM-associated molecular alterations at delivery. By integrating DIA proteomics, co-expression network analysis and pathway-level corroboration using independent transcriptomic datasets, the study identifies placental extracellular matrix remodeling and ribosome-related processes, while exploratory analyses of UCB suggest immune- and coagulation-related pathway patterns. These findings provide a basis for future hypothesis-driven studies of GDM-related placental dysfunction.

title: Interactive effect of childhood adversity and HPA-axis multilocus genetic variation on alexithymia in adolescents.
authors: Zhou H, Lü W
abstract: BACKGROUND: Childhood adversity increases risk for affective symptoms, including alexithymia, a transdiagnostic emotion-processing difficulty common in adolescence. Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis-related genetic variation may contribute to individual differences in sensitivity to adverse environments. This study examined whether an HPA-axis-related multilocus genetic profile score (MGPS) moderated the association between childhood adversity and adolescent alexithymia. METHODS: The present study addressed this issue in a sample of 460 adolescents (Mage = 12.73, SD = 0.72; 54.1% female) who completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire and the Toronto Alexithymia Scale. Saliva samples were collected for deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) genotyping, and an HPA-axis-related multilocus genetic profile score (MGPS) was constructed from six candidate polymorphisms. Hierarchical regression and re-parameterized regression analyses were conducted. RESULTS: Childhood adversity was positively associated with alexithymia. HPA-axis MGPS moderated this association. Specifically, adolescents with high HPA-axis MGPS exhibited higher levels of alexithymia when exposed to high childhood adversity but lower levels when exposed to low childhood adversity, providing preliminary support for the differential susceptibility model. LIMITATIONS: The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the findings require replication in longitudinal, clinically enriched, and more diverse samples. CONCLUSIONS: HPA-axis multilocus genetic variation may function as a biological sensitivity factor in the association between childhood adversity and adolescent alexithymia. These findings extend gene-environment interaction research to alexithymia and highlight individual differences in adolescents' emotional responses to adversity.

title: Environmental sensitivity and perceived social support in relation to adolescent eating disorder symptoms.
authors: Mastromatteo LY, Tosi C, Cardi V, Cerolini S, Meregalli V, Baglioni C, Scrimin S
abstract: Eating disorders (EDs) frequently emerge during adolescence and are influenced by both individual and contextual factors. Among these, perceived social support has generally been associated with better outcomes, although findings remain inconsistent and may depend on both the source of support and individual differences in responsiveness to environmental inputs. The present study examined the role of Environmental Sensitivity (ES) and perceived social support in adolescent ED symptoms, focusing on different sources of support and their potential interaction within a vantage sensitivity framework. A sample of 466 adolescents (51.61% female; M = 14.80) completed self-report measures of ED symptoms, ES, and perceived social support. At a bivariate level, higher perceived support from family, teachers, friends, and peers was associated with lower ED symptoms. In covariate-adjusted models, only teachers' and family's support remained a significant predictor, while peer-related sources were no longer associated with ED symptoms. ES was consistently and positively associated with ED symptoms. Contrary to hypotheses, ES did not moderate the association between overall perceived social support and ED symptoms. Exploratory analyses suggested a sex-specific pattern, whereby the association between perceived social support and ED symptoms appeared to vary as a function of ES among males, but not females. These findings suggest that the association between social support and adolescent ED symptoms may depend on its source. Moreover, ES was consistently associated with ED symptoms. Exploratory analyses revealed that evidence for differential responsiveness to supportive contexts may vary by ES among males.

title: Dynamic associations between help-seeking and suicidal ideation across family conflict contexts following psychiatric hospitalization.
authors: Anderson AS, Kudinova AY, Brick LA, Marraccini ME, Armey M, Nugent NR
abstract: Adolescents are at elevated risk for recurrent suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB) following discharge from psychiatric hospitalization, yet little is known about how help-seeking behaviors unfold dynamically during this high-risk transition period. Prior research suggests that family conflict may function both as a direct risk factor for STB and as an interpersonal context associated with how adolescents respond during periods of suicidal distress. Clarifying when adolescents are most likely to seek support, and how family context shapes these dynamic associations, is critical for informing intervention efforts. The present study used ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and time-varying effect modeling (TVEM) to examine dynamic associations between general problem-related help-seeking (i.e., talking to someone about one's problems) and suicidal ideation (SI) intensity during the three weeks following psychiatric hospitalization for STB in a sample of 96 adolescents (ages 13-18). Associations between SI and help-seeking were also examined across levels of family conflict. Help-seeking was positively associated with SI intensity early in the post-discharge period, with effects attenuating over time. Thus, adolescents may be more likely to seek support during moments of heightened distress shortly after returning to their environments. Associations differed by family context: adolescents reporting lower and average family conflict demonstrated stronger coupling between SI intensity and help-seeking, whereas no significant association emerged among adolescents reporting higher conflict. Findings suggest that help-seeking may be more closely aligned with periods of elevated distress early after hospitalization, particularly among adolescents with lower family conflict. Interventions that strengthen supportive relationships, particularly within family contexts, may facilitate help-seeking during this high-risk transition period.

title: Hypoxia-associated birth complications and offspring childhood internalizing, externalizing, and adolescent depression symptoms.
authors: Davies NL, Smith EC, Pike MR, Cunningham R, Cohn BA, Krigbaum NY, Cirillo P, Alloy LB
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Hypoxia-associated birth complications (termed fetal hypoxia, herein) have been linked with increased offspring schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorder, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, all comorbid with depression. The current study examined the contribution of fetal hypoxia exposure to adolescent depression symptoms through childhood internalizing and externalizing symptom pathways. METHODS: Included mother-offspring dyads (N = 1679) were drawn from a subset of the Child Health and Development Studies (CHDS). Participants were part of two follow-up studies during childhood (ages 9 to 11) and adolescence (ages 15 to 19). Fetal hypoxia exposure was assessed prospectively from pregnancy and birth medical visits. Childhood internalizing and externalizing symptoms were assessed through questionnaires completed by mothers, and adolescent depressive symptoms were assessed via offspring self-report. RESULTS: Exposure to fetal hypoxia significantly increased childhood internalizing symptoms, which were subsequently linked to heightened adolescent depression symptoms. Fetal hypoxia showed no significant direct association with adolescent depression and was not associated with childhood externalizing symptoms. CONCLUSION: Findings indicate that fetal hypoxia is linked to offspring childhood internalizing symptoms, which in turn, increased risk for adolescent depression symptoms. These findings add to preclinical and preliminary human evidence linking fetal hypoxia to offspring depression.
